name: Southeast Ridge
approach: From Winthrop, drive Highway 20 west about 14-15 miles to the Mazama junction, then either (a) continue on Lost River Road (County Road 9140) about 8.75 miles (paved then gravel Forest Road 5400) to Robinson Creek Trailhead, or (b) turn onto the Harts Pass Road (also FR-5400) and drive about 9.0 miles to the same trailhead (elev. ~2,500-2,560 ft, with an information sign, picnic table, and vault toilet). From the trailhead, hike the Robinson Creek - Middle Fork Trail (#478) north for about 2.8 miles to the signed/bridged Beauty Creek junction (elev. ~3,560 ft) just past a bridge over Beauty Creek. Turn right (northeast/uphill) onto the unmarked, overgrown Beauty Creek Trail and follow it about 1.5 miles up the valley, staying northwest of the creek, to a tributary crossing around 5,200-5,260 ft, then continue up open slopes to the tarn basin at about 6,750-6,800 ft.

road.name: Lost River Road (County Rd 9140) / Harts Pass Road (Forest Road 5400)
road.status: USFS-maintained gravel/paved road to the trailhead at ~2,500-2,560 ft; generally accessible spring through fall but has been subject to washout-related closures (e.g., closed into 2026 for flood/storm repairs before reopening in mid-2026).
road.driveNote: From Winthrop, drive Highway 20 west ~14-15 mi to the Mazama junction, then either continue on Lost River Road (~8.75 mi, pavement then gravel FR-5400) or turn onto Harts Pass Road (FR-5400) and drive ~9.0 mi to the Robinson Creek Trailhead on the right.

approach_variants.name: Robinson Creek #478 to the Beauty Creek trail #579, then the tarn basin
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Highway 20 west from Winthrop about fifteen miles, right onto Lost River Road, a half mile then left to stay on it, seven and a half paved miles and another mile and a quarter of gravel FR 5400 to the Robinson Creek trailhead on the right. The trailhead sits at 2,500 to 2,600 ft. Ballard Campground is a minute or two away and is the standard car-camp.

Walk the Robinson Creek trail #478 — an easy valley walk through big timber — about two and a half miles to the Beauty Creek junction near 3,560 to 3,600 ft. Mileages for it range from two to two and eight tenths, so use the elevation and the landmark rather than a mile count.

The landmark is the second bridge, the one over Beauty Creek, with Beauty Creek Falls cascading beside it. The junction is thirty to a hundred feet past that bridge, on the uphill side, and it is unmarked. Two parties independently warn that it is far less obvious than you would expect, one describing it as covered in bushes and nearly walked past. If you get thirty feet beyond the bridge and have not seen it, stop, go back, and look up on climber's right.

Beauty Creek #579 — not #479, which is a different trail entirely — is unmaintained and does not appear on maps. It stays on the west and north-west side of the creek the whole way. One party notes their topo showed it on the east side and the topo was wrong; that is a usable check. Blowdown is the recurring nuisance, typically five to nine logs.

Total for the peak is fourteen to fifteen miles with somewhere between 6,200 and 6,900 ft of gain, and four separate parties report ten to fourteen hours car to car as a single day.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep on rock. Earlier, with snow on the upper scree, is genuinely easier — the scree is the worst thing about this climb and snow removes it
hazards: An unmarked, bushy junction thirty to a hundred feet past the Beauty Creek bridge
Blowdown on an unmaintained trail that is not on maps
No water above the 6,700 ft tarn
A universally loathed scree slope with recorded party-inflicted rockfall — helmet
Fifty to sixty feet of exposed Class 3 just below the summit
approach_variants.baseFinding: The second transition is an unbridged creek, at about 5,200 to 5,260 ft. That creek is the outflow of the tarn you are heading for. Just a few feet past it the ground opens into meadow. Turn left, north-west, and go up. The boot path there is easy to miss — one climber walked past it thinking it was where a few goats had gone up the hill. About a hundred feet above the creek it turns into a well-worn track. If you cannot find it, do not hunt: several parties simply climbed north-west through the open meadow and reached the tarn anyway. Negative marker: if the Beauty Creek trail starts a gradual traverse below Robinson into the Beauty Creek headwaters, you have gone past the crossing. Arrival is a small heart-shaped tarn in a rocky basin at about 6,700 to 6,750 ft, sitting between two spur ridges, reached in fifteen hundred feet or so of climbing in well under a mile. This is the standard high camp and it is the last water — there is none above it. Above the tarn the ridge is gained somewhere between 7,400 and 7,600 ft depending on where you take it, up a scree slope that parties universally complain about. Carry patience and a helmet; there has been a near-miss from party-inflicted rockfall here. The false summit is Point 8,280. It sits north-west of the tarn, it looks exactly like the top, and the real summit is another half mile beyond it. The test is simple: if you top out and there is more ridge, more gendarmes and a higher point about half a mile to the north-west, you are on the 8,280 south-east peak. It can be sidehilled rather than climbed. The true crux comes just before the summit: a notch below the last false top, then about fifty to sixty feet of exposed Class 2-3 ridge. Two parties independently say the first five or six feet are the worst of it. Parties carry rock protection and do not place it. One disambiguation: Robinson Peak, above Harts Pass, is a different mountain a mile or so down the ridge from Robinson Mountain. Harts Pass is not an approach to this climb.
